content.text:
`high effort → 3+4 angles × 6 candidates → 1-vote verify (recall-biased) → ≤10 findings`

You are reviewing for **recall** at high effort: catch every real bug a careful
reviewer would catch in one sitting. At this level, catching real bugs matters
more than avoiding false positives. Err on the side of surfacing.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Find candidates (3 correctness angles + 3 cleanup angles + 1 altitude angle, up to 6 each)

Run **7 independent finder angles** via the Agent tool. Each
surfaces **up to 6 candidate findings** with `file`, `line`, a one-line
`summary`, and a concrete `failure_scenario`.

### Angle A — line-by-line diff scan

Read every hunk in the diff, line by line. Then Read the enclosing function for
each hunk — bugs in unchanged lines of a touched function are in scope (the PR
re-exposes or fails to fix them). For every line ask: what input, state, timing,
or platform makes this line wrong? Look for inverted/wrong conditions,
off-by-one, null/undefined deref, missing `await`, falsy-zero checks,
wrong-variable copy-paste, error swallowed in catch, unescaped regex metachars.

### Angle B — removed-behavior auditor

For every line the diff DELETES or replaces, name the invariant or behavior it
enforced, then search the new code for where that invariant is re-established.
If you can't find it, that's a candidate: a removed guard, a dropped error
path, a narrowed validation, a deleted test that was covering a real case.

### Angle C — cross-file tracer

For each function the diff changes, find its callers (Grep for the symbol) and
check whether the change breaks any call site: a new precondition, a changed
return shape, a new exception, a timing/ordering dependency. Also check callees:
does a parallel change in the same PR make a call unsafe?

### Reuse

The angles above hunt for bugs; this one and the next two hunt for cleanup in
the changed code. Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Name the cheaper alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

Cleanup and altitude candidates use the same `file`/`line`/`summary` shape; in
`failure_scenario`, state the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain) instead of a crash. Correctness bugs always outrank
cleanup and altitude findings when the output cap forces a cut.

Pass every candidate with a nameable failure scenario through — finders that
silently drop half-believed candidates bypass the verify step and are the
dominant cause of misses.

## Phase 2 — Verify (1-vote, recall-biased)

Dedup near-duplicates (same defect, same location, same reason → keep one). For
each remaining candidate, run **one verifier** via the Agent tool:
give it the diff, the relevant file(s), and the candidate; it returns exactly
one of **CONFIRMED / PLAUSIBLE / REFUTED**.

**PLAUSIBLE by default** — do not refute a candidate for being "speculative" or
"depends on runtime state" when the state is realistic: concurrency races,
nil/undefined on a rare-but-reachable path (error handler, cold cache, missing
optional field), falsy-zero treated as missing, off-by-one on a boundary the
code does not exclude, retry storms / partial failures, regex/allowlist that
lost an anchor. These are PLAUSIBLE.

**REFUTED** only when constructible from the code: factually wrong (quote the
actual line); provably impossible (type/constant/invariant — show it); already
handled in this diff (cite the guard); or pure style with no observable effect.

Keep **CONFIRMED and PLAUSIBLE**. Drop REFUTED.

## Output

Return findings as a JSON array of at most 10 objects:

```json
[
  {
    "file": "path/to/file.ext",
    "line": 123,
    "summary": "one-sentence statement of the bug",
    "failure_scenario": "concrete inputs/state → wrong output/crash"
  }
]
```

Ranked most-severe first. If more than 10 survive, keep the 10 most
severe. If nothing survives verification, return `[]`.

But `mirrorAdvertisesHead` does `defer resp.Body.Close()` without draining, and reads via `io.LimitReader`. Go's transport only recycles a connection when the body is read to EOF before `Close()`; on the `sr.Decode`/`adv.Decode` error returns (and possibly the normal path, depending on whether go-git consumes the trailing flush-pkt) the body is left partially read, so the conn is closed instead of pooled — every 2s probe then pays a fresh TLS handshake. Based on `parseGitHubURL` in `repo_mirror_probe.go:54-67` (and the command's own `Example` at `repo_mirror.go:123`), `entire repo mirror create <github-url>` accepts **GitHub repos only**, in three URL shapes:

| Shape | Regex | Example |
|---|---|---|
| HTTPS | `gitHubHTTPSRe` | `https://github.com/octocat/hello-world` (also `http://`, optional `.git`) |
| SSH | `gitHubSSHRe` | `git@github.com:octocat/hello-world.git` |
| Bare | `gitHubBareRe` | `octocat/hello-world` or `github.com/octocat/hello-world` |

All three allow an optional trailing `.git`. The matched `owner`/`repo` are lowercased to match the server's persisted `/gh/<owner>/<repo>` slug.

**Constraints on owner/repo** (deliberately matched to GitHub's real identifier charset, not "anything but slash"):
- **owner**: `[A-Za-z0-9-]+` — letters, digits, hyphens. No dots, no underscores.
- **repo**: `[A-Za-z0-9._-]+?` — letters, digits, dots, underscores, hyphens; **but rejected if entirely dots** (`.`, `..`, …) via the `gitHubDotOnlyRe` check this branch added.

Anything else is rejected at the CLI boundary with `not a recognized GitHub URL` (or the dot-only message). The reason for the tight charset, per the comment at `repo_mirror_probe.go:28-35`: owner/repo flow unescaped into the STS token audience and the smart-HTTP probe URL, so a permissive pattern would let names like `repo?bypass=1` or `repo#x` smuggle query strings / truncate paths.

So: **no GitLab, Bitbucket, arbitrary git hosts, or self-hosted URLs** — only `github.com`. The optional second arg is the cluster host (e.g. `eu-west-1.entire.io`), not a repo URL.

## Review: PR #1305 — Add `entire blame` and `entire why` commands

**Overall: a substantial, well-structured, well-tested feature (+1432 lines, 318 of them tests).** The design is clean — a single `attributionResolver` with commit/checkpoint caching, sensible AI/Human/Mixed/Uncommitted classification, stable JSON output, and good reuse of the existing checkpoint/trailers/explain infrastructure. No blocking bugs. The findings below are real but minor — robustness, efficiency, and cleanup, none of which should hold up the merge.

### Findings (ranked)

**1. `git blame` parser only matches SHA-1 object IDs** — `attribution.go:594` (low / robustness)
`blameHeaderRe = ^([0-9a-f]{40})...` hardcodes 40 hex chars. On a SHA-256 repo (`git init --object-format=sha256`, 64-hex IDs), no header matches, `parseBlamePorcelain` returns an empty slice with no error, and `entire blame`/`why` silently print "No lines to display." Use `[0-9a-f]{40,64}` (or `[0-9a-f]+`). Low priority if the codebase assumes SHA-1 everywhere, but this fails *silently*, which is the worst failure mode.

**2. `entire why <file>:<line> --json` opens the repo twice** — `attribution.go:464-472` (low / efficiency)
`resolveFileAttribution` already builds a resolver (repo + GitStore + caches). When a selected line is `MetadataMissing`, `enrichAttributionLineWithFetch` opens a *second* resolver with `fetchOnMiss=true` and rebuilds everything. The codebase already has the cheaper pattern: `fetchCheckpointContext` (`:531-537`) temporarily flips `r.store`/`r.fetchOnMiss` on the existing resolver and restores them. Thread the existing resolver through instead of opening a new one.

**3. Duplicated candidate-copy logic** — `attribution.go:345-379` and `474-512` (maintainability)
Two near-identical blocks copy an `attributionCheckpointContext` → `attributionCandidate` (9 fields) and then a preferred candidate → `attributionLine` fields (7 fields). A field added to either struct must be mirrored in both. Extract `candidateFromContext(ctx)` and `applyPreferred(line, cand)` helpers.

**4. Fields written but never read** — `attribution.go:63, 88, 83` (cleanup)
`attributionLine.CheckpointIDs`, `attributionCheckpointContext.SessionIDs`, and `attributionCandidate.Mixed` are populated but only ever surface via `omitempty` JSON — no rendering or branching consumes them (line-level `Mixed` decisions use the *context's* `Mixed`, not the candidate's). If they're part of the intended stable JSON contract, add a comment saying so; otherwise drop them.

**5. Re-implemented helpers + an inconsistency** — `attribution.go:1060, 1098` (reuse)
`writeJSON` (encoder + `SetIndent("", "  ")` + `Encode`) is duplicated across `sessions.go`, `explain_export.go`, `trail_cmd.go` — worth a shared helper. More notably, `shortSHA` truncates to **8** chars while `explain.go` uses **7** for the same display concept — minor, but it means the same commit prints differently across two commands.

**6. Checkpoint-resolution overlaps `explain.go`** — `attribution.go:397-462` (altitude, discretionary)
`readCheckpointContext` (ReadCommittedCheckpoint + session enumeration + prompt selection) parallels logic in `explain.go`, and `fetchCheckpointContext` reaches into `newExplainCheckpointLookup`/`matchCheckpointPrefixWithRemoteFallback` to fetch on miss. It works, but a shared "build checkpoint context for a checkpoint ID" helper would keep blame/why/explain from drifting. Worth considering, not required now.

### Verified non-issues
- `resolver.Close()` → `repo.Close()` is correct (fresh repo per `openRepository`).
- Separator width `lineWidth+92` aligns exactly with the header (a finder miscounted).
- `parseAttributionLineRange` and the Windows-volume handling in `parseAttributionWhyTarget` are solid. One tiny edge: a colon-containing filename with no line (`entire why weird:name.go`) errors as `invalid line target` — rare and arguably acceptable.

Want me to push any of these as inline PR comments (#1–2 are the only ones I'd genuinely gate on), or leave the review here?

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Name the cheaper alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

Four cleanup agents reviewed the PR #1305 diff; I deduped their findings and applied the high-confidence ones. Net: **−31 lines** in `attribution.go` (42 insertions, 73 deletions), build + lint + tests all green.

1. **Extracted `candidateFromContext`** — collapsed two identical 9-field `attributionCheckpointContext → attributionCandidate` copy blocks (in `resolveLine` and `enrichAttributionLineWithFetch`). Lint revealed the structs are now field-identical, so it's a one-line `attributionCandidate(ctx)` conversion that fails loudly at compile time if they ever diverge.
2. **Extracted `applyPreferredToLine`** — collapsed two identical 7-field preferred-candidate→line copy blocks. Authorship/Mixed handling stays at each call site since it differs.
3. **Extracted `renderByAuthorship`** — `renderAttributionTag` and `renderAttributionContent` had the same authorship→colour switch; now both delegate to one helper.

6. **`isZeroCommit`** — replaced the 40-zero string literal with `plumbing.ZeroHash.String()`.

### Skipped (with reasons)
- **`candidate.Mixed` "dead field"** — false positive; it's read at `resolveLine` (`if preferred.Mixed`). Kept.
- **`enrichAttributionLineWithFetch` reopens the repo** (efficiency) — real, but only on the cold "metadata missing + remote fetch" path, and the fix restructures resolver ownership/lifecycle. Not worth the correctness risk in a quality-only pass.

- **`shortSHA` 8 vs `explain.go`'s 7 chars**, **SHA-256 regex**, **`normalizePathSlice`/`appendUniqueString` vs `state.go` equivalents** — either change user-visible output, are correctness/robustness items (out of scope for /simplify), or have genuinely different contracts.
